bull_thesis: Olema is one molecule and one experiment, and the experiment is close. Palazestrant is a once-daily pill for the most common form of advanced breast cancer, the kind that grows in response to oestrogen. It is designed to shut the oestrogen receptor down completely, blocking both of the receptor's switches and degrading the receptor itself, where the pills already on the market reliably block only one. The pivotal study, OPERA-01, enrolled about 510 patients whose disease had already progressed on hormone therapy plus a CDK4/6 inhibitor, and it tests palazestrant on its own against whatever single hormone drug the treating doctor would otherwise choose. Management guided to top-line results in the fall of 2026 when it reported first-quarter figures on 12 May 2026, and the trial registry lists an estimated primary completion date of 30 June 2026 that has now passed on schedule. Nothing in the record shows that guidance being softened or pushed. The bullish case rests on three things the market is not paying for. First, the trial is built to win broadly. Its results are reported separately in patients whose tumours carry an ESR1 mutation, a genetic change that develops under hormone therapy in roughly four of ten patients, and separately in patients who do not carry it. Olema could have registered a mutation-only study and secured a likely approval in a small niche; it deliberately took on the harder population, which is where the whole prize sits. Second, the comparator is weak. These are patients on their second or third line of treatment, measured against a single hormone drug, which historically buys them only a couple of months before the disease grows again. Third, the balance sheet removes the usual way biotech investors lose money before a readout. Olema held $505.4 million of cash and marketable securities against $3.96 million of total debt at 31 March 2026, with no term loan, no convertible note, no covenant and no going-concern language. It does not need to raise money before the answer arrives, and the only shares it has issued this year are routine new-hire option grants. There is a second asset that costs nothing at today's price. OP-3136, aimed at an enzyme called KAT6, showed no dose-limiting toxicities up to 45 mg daily in its first human study reported on 21 May 2026, with tumour shrinkage observed, and on 26 May 2026 Bayer agreed to run a joint study combining it with its prostate-cancer drug darolutamide. A large pharmaceutical company put its own medicine next to Olema's. The final piece is behavioural. On 17 July 2026 Olema registered a second Phase 3 study, about 1,000 patients, testing palazestrant with ribociclib as a first treatment. That is an expensive commitment made months before the validating result. Management cannot see the unblinded data, so it is confidence rather than knowledge, but confidence expressed through spending carries more weight than confidence expressed in a press release. For the bull case to pay, one condition must hold: palazestrant must show a clear delay in disease progression in the patients without an ESR1 mutation, not only in those who have it. If it does, Olema owns the first all-comers oral endocrine therapy after CDK4/6 treatment, in a market where every existing option is confined to the mutation-positive minority.
bear_thesis: The bear case is short and it is specific: the drug class has been tested twice in exactly this way, and twice it has won only in the mutation-positive minority. Elacestrant, and more recently Lilly's imlunestrant tested as a single agent after a CDK4/6 inhibitor, both produced convincing results in patients carrying an ESR1 mutation and both failed to establish a clear benefit in the wider population. That is the population OPERA-01 must win to justify anything close to today's price. Olema's answer is mechanistic, not empirical: palazestrant blocks both of the receptor's switches, so in theory it should work whether or not the mutation is present. That theory has never survived a Phase 3. Four months ago the class produced a further warning. Roche's persevERA study of giredestrant, a drug working through the same receptor, enrolled 992 patients, reached its primary completion date on 30 January 2026 and did not succeed against letrozole plus palbociclib in first-line patients. The setting differs from OPERA-01 in line of therapy, comparator and the use of a combination rather than monotherapy, so it is not a direct read-across. But it establishes that this mechanism can lose a large, well-funded, well-designed trial. Olema's shares fell hard on it and have drifted from roughly $17 to $12.01 since, now sitting 31% below their own 200-day average of $17.44. The more uncomfortable point is what the likely outcome is worth. If palazestrant wins only in the mutation-positive group, Olema becomes the third or fourth entrant into a niche that elacestrant and imlunestrant already serve and that AstraZeneca's camizestrant is entering, addressing perhaps four in ten of these patients, with no pricing power and a commercial build to fund from scratch. That outcome is worth roughly what the stock costs today. In other words, the single most likely result pays the buyer nothing. Cash is being consumed faster into the event, not slower. Operating cash outflow rose from $29.9 million in the June 2025 quarter to $46.0 million in the March 2026 quarter, and the company has since started a 1,000-patient first-line study that is worthless if OPERA-01 fails and costly to unwind. By the readout, cash should be near $400 million rather than $505 million. Finally, the published expectations are stale and unreliable as a guide. Twelve analysts carry an average price target of $40.70 against a $12.01 share price, with only one published number, LifeSci Capital's $23, anywhere near where the stock trades. Those models were built for a broad success and have not been re-underwritten since March 2026. A gap that wide is not an opportunity signal; it is evidence that the sell-side has stopped marking its work, and it means there is no institutional support level beneath the stock if the data disappoint. What would confirm the bear case: any softening of the fall-2026 language, a result that reports a benefit only in the mutation-positive analysis, or an equity raise before the data.
sop_bull: Event-win value of about $30 per share. Against an addressable second-and-later-line population of that size and typical branded oncology pricing, peak annual sales of $1.0 to $1.5 billion are supportable. sop_bear: Verified downside floor of about $4.25 per share, materially below the board file's working floor of $6.50, which is not supportable. sop_breakdown: Probability-weighted across three discrete outcomes, because the honest distribution here has two humps rather than a smooth range. Broad win, meaning a clear delay in disease progression in both the mutation-positive and the mutation-negative populations: 25% probability, $30 per share. This is the outcome the trial was deliberately designed to chase and the only one that justifies the sell-side's models. Narrow win, meaning a clear result in mutation-positive patients only: 45% probability, $13 per share. risk_reward: Upside to the $24 event-win target is plus 100% from $12.01. Downside to the verified $4.25 floor is minus 65%. That is about 1.5 to 1 on the two tails. An investor is effectively paying par for the middle case in order to hold a 25% ticket on a double, against a 30% chance of losing about two-thirds. That is a legitimate defined-risk binary, not a bargain, and it must be sized accordingly.
catalyst_summary: Top-line results from the 510-patient pivotal OPERA-01 study of palazestrant, guided to the fall of 2026 on 12 May 2026 and never softened, with the trial's registered maturity date of 30 June 2026 already passed: about 100% upside to a $24 event-win value against roughly 65% downside to a $4.25 floor backed by around $400 million of unencumbered cash and no debt.

Only one published number, LifeSci Capital's $23, is anywhere near the tape. That is what the market is paying for a pivotal-stage oncology asset reading out within four months in one of the largest cancer indications there is, plus a Bayer-partnered second molecule, plus the free option that a mutation-only win still creates a real, saleable product. Nearly half the share price is cash. The market has moved from pricing the broad win as likely to pricing it as close to an afterthought, and 17.29% of the shares outstanding are sold short. moderator_conclusion: Buy it now, in small size, and hold it as a binary rather than an investment. This is what the event-driven funnel exists to find, and it clears the structural test cleanly. interrogator_dossier:
# Olema Oncology (OLMA) — Forensic Dossier on an Event, Not a Franchise

*Prepared 28 July 2026. All prices and balance-sheet figures verified against public sources
on 27–28 July 2026. This is an event-driven special situation: the question is not whether
Olema is a good business — it has no revenue and no business yet — but whether one specific
experiment is real, dated, and binding, and what actually backstops the share price if it fails.*

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Olema has spent five years narrowing rather than broadening. What began as a discovery platform
is now, in practical terms, one molecule and one experiment.

The molecule is palazestrant (internal code OP-1250), a once-daily pill for the most common form
of advanced breast cancer — tumours that grow in response to oestrogen (the medical shorthand is
"ER-positive, HER2-negative"). Roughly seven in ten breast cancers are of this type. Palazestrant
is designed to shut the oestrogen receptor down completely: it blocks both of the receptor's two
switches and also degrades the receptor itself. The competing pills on the market block only one
switch reliably.

The experiment is OPERA-01, registry number NCT06016738. I read the trial record directly on
28 July 2026. It is a Phase 3, open-label, randomised study of about 510 patients whose disease
has already progressed on hormone therapy plus a CDK4/6 inhibitor (the standard first-line
combination, drugs such as palbociclib or ribociclib). Palazestrant on its own is measured against
whatever single hormone drug the treating doctor would otherwise choose — fulvestrant, anastrozole,
letrozole or exemestane. The endpoint is progression-free survival, meaning how long patients live
before the cancer grows again, judged by an independent review panel that does not know which drug
each patient received.

The single most important design detail, and the one the market discusses least: OPERA-01 reads out
in **two separate populations** — patients whose tumours carry an ESR1 mutation (a specific genetic
change that develops under hormone therapy and appears in roughly 40% of these patients), and,
separately, patients whose tumours do **not** carry it. Olema is not hedging its bet into a
mutation-only label. It is explicitly testing the harder claim.

The narrative has also quietly acquired a second leg. In May 2026 the company reported first
human data on OP-3136, a different molecule aimed at an enzyme called KAT6, with no dose-limiting
toxicities up to 45 mg daily and some tumour shrinkage observed. On 26 May 2026 Bayer agreed to
run a joint Phase 1b/2 study combining OP-3136 with its prostate-cancer drug darolutamide in about
36 patients, starting in the second half of 2026. That is a small collaboration, but a real
pharmaceutical company put its name and its drug next to Olema's.

And there is a third development that cuts both ways. On 17 July 2026 the registry was updated for
NCT07085767 — a **new, second Phase 3 trial**, roughly 1,000 patients, testing palazestrant combined
with ribociclib as a *first* treatment, with completion estimated December 2028. Olema is spending
money on a 1,000-patient study before the 510-patient study that validates the drug has reported.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

There are no revenues to test a growth claim against. The claims that matter here are about
solvency, timing, and credibility — and those are testable.

| Management's claim | What the numbers actually show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Top-line data from the pivotal Phase 3 OPERA-01 trial in fall 2026" (stated with Q1 results, 12 May 2026) | The trial registry lists an estimated primary completion date of 30 June 2026 — already passed. Data cleaning and independent-panel adjudication typically take two to four months. A September-to-November announcement is arithmetically consistent, not aspirational. | **Corroborated** |
| The company is fully funded through the readout | $505.35M in cash and marketable securities at 31 March 2026 against $3.96M of total debt. Cash burn from operations was $46.0M in the March 2026 quarter (prior four quarters: $38.3M, $34.5M, $29.9M, $44.0M). Two more quarters at a rising ~$50M leaves roughly $400M at the readout. | **Corroborated, comfortably** |
| No dilution required before the event | No equity offering appears in the 2026 news record. The only share issuances disclosed are routine new-hire option grants — 176,150 shares at $12.71 on 2 June 2026 and 215,800 shares at $12.08 on 2 July 2026. A company quietly hiring is not a company preparing a rescue financing. | **Corroborated** |
| The drug works regardless of ESR1 mutation status | This is the load-bearing claim and it is **not yet supported by any Phase 3 evidence anywhere in the drug class.** It rests on mechanism and on mid-stage data. It is exactly what OPERA-01 is designed to answer. | **Unproven — this is the bet** |

The balance sheet deserves emphasis because it is the only thing standing between an investor and
zero. Enterprise value — market capitalisation minus net cash — is about **$548M** against a
$1.05B market capitalisation at $12.01 per share on 27 July 2026. Put plainly: **just under half
of what you pay for this share is cash sitting in the bank**, and there is essentially no debt
against it. Net cash works out to $5.74 per share today and roughly $4.55 per share by the time
the data arrive.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Stable, and stable in a way that is itself evidence.** The tell is not what management says but
what it has not done. Guidance for OPERA-01 data has pointed at the second half of 2026 and then
specifically at the fall, and I can find no instance of that guidance being walked back, softened
to "around year-end", or converted to "when the required number of events accrue" — the standard
euphemism a biotech reaches for when a trial is running behind. On 12 May 2026 the language was
still direct: top-line data in fall 2026.

The other tone signal is behavioural. Launching a second, 1,000-patient Phase 3 in the first-line
setting in July 2026 — months before the validating readout — is not defensive language. It is a
capital commitment that only makes sense if management believes the first trial will succeed.
Management does not see unblinded results, so this is confidence, not knowledge. But confidence
backed by spending is worth more than confidence expressed in a press release.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**High, on the narrow question of timing.** The relevant track record is not earnings beats — there
are no earnings — but whether stated dates have held. They have. The fall-2026 window has been
reiterated rather than revised, the trial's registered maturity date has been reached on schedule,
and the balance sheet removes the most common reason a small biotech quietly delays a readout,
which is that it needs to raise money into a stronger tape first.

One genuine housekeeping gap: the OPERA-01 registry record still shows a status of "Recruiting"
with a verification date of August 2025, and was last updated 13 March 2026. For a trial the company
says will report this autumn, that record is stale. Registry lag is common and I do not read it as
concealment, but it is the sort of untidiness that leaves an investor relying on the company's word
rather than an independent timestamp.

**Reliability: High on timing. Unknown on outcome — and the outcome is what is being priced.**

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

The sell-side is not pressuring management at all, and that is the problem. Twelve analysts cover
the stock. Nine rate it strong buy, two buy, one hold. The average price target is **$40.70**, with
a median of $40, a low of $23 (LifeSci Capital) and a high of $62. The shares closed at **$12.01**
on 27 July 2026.

A consensus target more than three times the market price is not a forecast. It is a set of models
that were built for a broad success and have not been re-underwritten since March 2026, when Roche's
persevERA trial of the same-class drug giredestrant reported. That trial — registry number
NCT04546009, 992 patients, primary completion 30 January 2026, record last updated 19 May 2026 —
tested giredestrant plus palbociclib against letrozole plus palbociclib in first-line patients and
did not succeed. Olema's shares fell sharply and have since drifted from roughly $17 to $12, with
the 200-day average now at $17.44. The targets did not move with the price. Only one of twelve
analysts has published a number anywhere near where the stock trades.

The question no one is pressing management on publicly is the one that decides the trade: what
happens to the wild-type population — the roughly 60% of patients without an ESR1 mutation — given
that no oral drug in this class has yet won there.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **The class has a consistent, unhelpful pattern.** Elacestrant and, more recently, Lilly's
imlunestrant both won convincingly in ESR1-mutant patients and both failed to establish a clear
benefit in the wider population — imlunestrant in essentially OPERA-01's own setting, as a single
agent after a CDK4/6 inhibitor. Two attempts, two mutation-only outcomes. Olema is attempting
precisely the thing the class has not yet done.

🔴 **A same-mechanism Phase 3 failed four months ago.** persevERA is not a perfect read-across —
different line of therapy, different comparator, a combination rather than monotherapy — but it
demonstrates that this receptor-blocking mechanism can lose a large, well-funded Phase 3.

🔴 **The board file's downside floor of $6.50 per share is not supportable.** Net cash is $5.74 per
share *today* and will be roughly $4.55 by the readout. A floor above current net cash implies the
market would pay a premium to cash for a company that had just failed its pivotal trial. It would not.

🔴 **Burn is accelerating into the event.** Operating cash outflow rose from $29.9M in the June 2025
quarter to $46.0M in the March 2026 quarter, and a 1,000-patient first-line study has since started.
That trial has no value if OPERA-01 fails, and unwinding it would cost money.

🟢 **No financing risk before the catalyst.** $505M of unencumbered cash, $3.96M of debt, no term
loan, no convertible, no covenant, no going-concern language. The single most common way a biotech
investor loses money before the data — a dilutive rescue raise at a distressed price — is off the
table here.

🟢 **The positioning is already washed out.** Short interest stands at **15.10 million shares, or
17.29% of shares outstanding.** The 52-week range runs from $4.47 to $36.26 against $12.01 today.
The optimistic shareholder base largely left after March 2026; what remains is heavily shorted and
trading 31% below its own 200-day average. Bad news is at least partly in the price. Good news is
not.

🟢 **Genuine residual value if the main drug fails.** OP-3136 has clean initial safety data
(no dose-limiting toxicities to 45 mg), observed responses, and a named partner in Bayer as of
26 May 2026. That is not a rounding error against a busted-biotech valuation.

🟢 **Management has spent its own capital on the outcome.** The July 2026 first-line study is a
costly expression of belief made before the answer is known.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most informative detail in the entire file is the trial's dual-population design. Olema could
have registered OPERA-01 to read out in mutation-positive patients alone, matched the approved
competition, and secured a high-probability approval in a modest niche. It did not. It registered
a separate primary analysis in mutation-negative patients — the population where the class has
failed. That is a deliberate decision to make the trial harder in exchange for a far larger prize,
and it is why the outcome distribution here is genuinely two-humped rather than a smooth range.

The second signal is what routine hiring implies. Granting new-employee options in both June and
July 2026, at $12.71 and $12.08, tells you a company still building a team on the assumption it
will have something to sell.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.** Nothing about the setup has deteriorated operationally. What changed in
March 2026 was the market's estimate of the odds, not Olema's execution.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** this is not a range of outcomes, it is
three discrete ones, and the middle one is worth roughly today's price. A broad win covering both
mutation groups is worth somewhere near $30 per share. A narrow win in mutation-positive patients
only makes Olema the third or fourth entrant into a niche two rivals already serve, worth perhaps
$13. A clean failure leaves cash and an early-stage second molecule, worth about $4.25. The
probability-weighted middle sits a little above the current price, but the *most likely single
outcome* pays roughly nothing from here. Size this as a defined-risk binary — the position must be
small enough that a 65% loss to the cash floor is an acceptable outcome, because that is a live
branch, not a tail.

**Moat:** none, and the question is not really applicable. Olema has no franchise, no customers and
no revenue. What patent protection and mechanism differentiation exist are potential assets that
only become a moat if the trial succeeds. **Secular threat: manageable** — advanced breast cancer
is a growing, well-reimbursed market with no structural force eroding it; the risk here is
competitive and scientific, not secular. The cheapness on conventional metrics is by design and
carries no information.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 3 | TRAJECTORY: STABLE | MOAT: NONE | MOAT_TREND: STABLE | SECULAR_THREAT: manageable
skeptic_kill_fact: The catalyst survives verification cleanly, but every per-share number in the file is inflated by roughly 15 percent because the wrong share count is used, and correcting it erases the stated edge. Olema's 10-Q (filed 12 May 2026) reports 87,347,471 common shares outstanding as of 7 May 2026 and states that this figure EXCLUDES 13,594,149 shares issuable on pre-funded warrants that are immediately exercisable at $0.0001 and already paid for. The company treats them as outstanding for its own accounts: Q1-2026 weighted-average shares used for EPS were 102,800,098, a figure I verified independently against the filed income statement (net loss $53,089k, EPS -$0.52). The file nonetheless divides net cash by 87.35 million and the win case by 'about 90 million shares'. On the correct ~101 million fully-paid base the file's own inputs give: net cash $501.4M = $4.97 per share today, not $5.74; the file's own $400M at readout = $3.96 per share, not $4.55; and applying the file's own 0.8-0.9x post-failure multiple plus its OP-3136 credit gives a floor near $3.75, not $4.25 -- downside from $12.01 is about 69 percent, not 65. The same denominator deflates the upside: the file's $2.7-3.2bn equity value divided by ~103M shares at readout is roughly $26, not $30, and the narrow-win branch ($1.0-1.2bn) is roughly $10.50, not $13. Reweighting the file's own probabilities (0.25 x $26 + 0.45 x $10.50 + 0.30 x $3.75) gives about $12.35 against a $12.01 price. The '+21 percent edge to a $14.50 fair value' that the moderator used to justify the position is therefore approximately +3 percent. The floor does NOT break -- the cash is verified, there is no going-concern qualification, no convertible and no financing contingency before the data -- and the tails remain roughly 1.45:1 with the $24 event-win target intact, so this is a correction rather than a kill. But the position must not be sized on the file's arithmetic. Separately, two material errors flagged in the prior skeptic pass remain UNABSORBED in this board file and are repeated verbatim: the claim that 'the only shares it has issued this year are routine new-hire option grants' (the 10-Q shows 1,712,739 shares sold for $41.9M net under a live TD Cowen ATM in Q1 2026, which is why cash was flat at ~$505M while the company burned $46M), and the claim of 'no term loan, no covenant' with assets unencumbered (a senior secured SVB/First-Citizens facility of up to $100.0M, $3.0M drawn, most recently amended 11 January 2026, is 'secured by substantially all of the assets of the Company').
